golden_comments.comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

When a user disables 2FA using a backup code, the backup code is validated but never removed from the database. Backup codes are generated using crypto.randomBytes(5).toString('hex'), producing only 10 hex characters (40 bits of entropy). Two concurrent login requests with the same backup code can both succeed because the read-check-delete sequence is not atomic. Both requests read the same backup codes from the database, both find the code at the same index, both set it to null, and both update the database. The second update overwrites the first with the same data, allowing the backup code to be used twice.

https://github.com/calcom/cal.com/pull/1.pr_title: OAuth credential sync and app integration enhancements

golden_comments.comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
Invalid Zod schema syntax. Computed property keys like [z.string().toString()] are not valid in Zod object schemas and will cause runtime errors.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

review_comments.body:
[High] Webhook endpoint allows creating/updating credentials for any user without authorization

The new webhook endpoint at /api/webhook/app-credential allows external systems to create or update app credentials for any user by simply providing a userId. There is no authorization check to verify that the caller has permission to manage credentials for that specific user. The only authentication is the webhook secret header. If an attacker obtains the webhook secret (e.g., through misconfiguration, logging, or source code exposure), they can create credentials for any user, effectively gaining access to all their third-party integrations (Google Calendar, Office365, Salesforce, etc.).

[Medium] Token validation weakened when credential sharing is enabled

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is true, the parseRefreshTokenResponse function uses a minimal schema that only validates the presence of access_token and a numeric property (expiry). This bypasses app-specific token validation schemas (e.g., googleCredentialSchema, refreshTokenResponseSchema). Additionally, if refresh_token is missing from the response, it's hardcoded to the string 'refresh_token', which is a placeholder value that would break token refresh functionality.

[High] Invalid Zod schema for minimumTokenResponseSchema

The schema uses `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` which is not valid Zod syntax for defining a catch-all property. This will cause a runtime error when Zod tries to parse the schema definition. The correct approach would be to use `.catchall(z.number())` on an object schema.

[High] Placeholder string instead of actual refresh token

When `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token` is falsy, the code sets it to the literal string `"refresh_token"` instead of the actual refresh token value. This will cause authentication failures because subsequent token refreshes will use this placeholder string instead of a valid refresh token.

[Medium] External credential sync endpoint introduces SSRF and information disclosure risk

When credential sharing is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens makes a POST request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT with calcomUserId and appSlug. This endpoint URL is configurable via environment variable and could be set to an attacker-controlled server. The function sends user IDs and app information to this external endpoint, and the response is used directly without validation of the endpoint's identity or response integrity.

[Medium] Salesforce CalendarService refresh token handling may lose refresh_token

The new Salesforce CalendarService code fetches a new access token but only saves the parsed response data, which may not include a refresh_token. The code manually adds the old refresh_token back, but if the Salesforce API returns a new refresh_token (which is common in OAuth2), it will be lost. This could cause token refresh to fail after the first refresh cycle.

[High] Blocking HTTP fetch in CalendarService constructor

The constructor of SalesforceCalendarService now makes a synchronous HTTP POST request to refresh OAuth tokens before returning the connection object. This fetch is blocking and happens every time a SalesforceCalendarService is instantiated, which occurs on every calendar operation (list events, create event, update event, delete event) for Salesforce users. Previously the constructor was purely synchronous, setting up connection parameters. Now it adds ~200-500ms of latency to every calendar operation for Salesforce users.

[High] Token refresh result not used in connection creation

The constructor fetches a new access token and updates the credential in the database, but then creates the jsforce.Connection using the original `credentialKey` values (which may have expired tokens). The refreshed token from the fetch is not passed to the connection constructor.

[Medium] Zoho Bigin CalendarService passes credentialId instead of userId to refreshOAuthTokens

The refreshOAuthTokens function expects a userId parameter, but the Zoho Bigin CalendarService passes credentialId (which is the credential's ID, not the user's ID). This means the external sync endpoint would receive a credential ID instead of a user ID, potentially causing incorrect data to be sent to the sync endpoint.

[High] Inconsistent return type from refreshOAuthTokens

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function returns different types depending on the code path: when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is true, it returns a fetch Response object; when false, it returns the result of the callback (which for Google Calendar is `fetchTokens.res` - the Google auth response data). The code then does `const token = res?.data;` which works for the Google auth response but would fail for a fetch Response (which has `.data` as undefined).

The addGuests mutation has no rate limiting, allowing an authenticated user to add unlimited guests to a booking in rapid succession. This could lead to email flooding, calendar spam, and resource exhaustion.

The input schema accepts an array of email strings with no maximum length validation. An attacker could send a request with thousands of email addresses, potentially causing resource exhaustion and abuse.

[Medium] O(n) iteration over offset range in get_committable_offsets

The get_committable_offsets method iterates over every offset from last_committed+1 to max_offset to find contiguous completed offsets. This is O(range_size) where range_size can be millions if there are large gaps in offsets (e.g., due to retries, out-of-order delivery, or slow processing). This runs every 1 second in the commit thread, creating a CPU bottleneck at high throughput. For a partition with offsets 0-1,000,000 where only 0-100 are committed, this iterates 999,900 times per second.

[High] Unbounded memory growth in OffsetTracker for partitions with offset gaps

The OffsetTracker stores all offsets in sets per partition. If offsets are never committed due to gaps (e.g., offset 100 completes but 99 is still outstanding), the all_offsets set grows unbounded. The mark_committed method only removes offsets <= committed offset, but gaps prevent cleanup. Over hours/days of operation with high-throughput topics, this can consume gigabytes of memory.

[Medium] Unbounded queue growth under backpressure

The queue.Queue instances in FixedQueuePool are created without a maxsize parameter, making them unbounded. If worker threads are slower than the producer (e.g., due to slow result_processor calls), queues grow indefinitely, leading to OOM. There is no backpressure mechanism to slow down the producer when queues are full.

[Medium] Race condition in worker shutdown

In FixedQueuePool.shutdown(), worker.shutdown is set to True without synchronization, and workers check self.shutdown without synchronization. A worker could check shutdown, find it False, then block on work_queue.get() before shutdown is set. The queue.shutdown() call should unblock it, but there's a race where the worker might not see the shutdown flag and block indefinitely.

However, in production, create_thread_queue_parallel_worker wraps the commit function to add +1 to each offset, so the actual committed offset would be 105.
